frictionVectors.title: EU Gas Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Europe remains a crucial market for Algerian gas, creating mutual dependence but exposing Algiers to pricing, infrastructure, and political pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Algeria's rivalry with Morocco continues to shape regional diplomacy, border security, and competing energy and transport corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Oil Dominance
frictionVectors.details: International firms retain major roles in offshore production and technology, while declining output constrains Luanda's bargaining power and fiscal space.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-Backed Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese financing and construction remain important for transport and energy projects, raising long-term concerns over debt exposure and strategic dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Niger Border Dispute
frictionVectors.details: Political tensions with Niger threaten port access, regional trade, and energy logistics, increasing Benin's vulnerability to decisions made beyond its borders.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Insurgency
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist violence and cross-border trafficking are pressuring northern communities and drawing greater reliance on external security support.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Botswana has improved its negotiating position with De Beers, but diamond marketing, expertise, and global demand still constrain full value-chain sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Competition
frictionVectors.details: Interest in Botswana's copper, nickel, and other minerals is growing, creating opportunities for diversification alongside pressure to offer favorable terms to foreign investors.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Partnership
frictionVectors.details: Closer security cooperation with Russia may reduce Western influence, but opaque arrangements risk substituting one external dependency for another.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-Sector Fragmentation
frictionVectors.details: Artisanal mining, smuggling, and insurgent taxation weaken state oversight of gold resources and divert revenues from formal public institutions.

frictionVectors.title: Opaque Gold and Nickel Chains
frictionVectors.details: Gold smuggling and weak traceability limit state capture of mineral revenues. The stalled nickel sector remains dependent on foreign capital, infrastructure, and export access.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda-DRC Security Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Tensions involving Rwanda and armed networks in eastern DRC constrain border trade and sovereignty. Burundi remains reliant on external diplomatic and security relationships while managing regional pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Connectivity
frictionVectors.details: Ports, airports, digital networks, and renewable-energy projects depend heavily on European, Chinese, and other external finance. This expands access and resilience but limits domestic control over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Atlantic Maritime Security
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde's location exposes it to narcotics trafficking, illegal fishing, and competing external maritime-security agendas. Enforcement capacity is improving but remains dependent on foreign partners.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms and lenders remain central to roads, hydropower, ports, and mining-linked infrastructure. Debt exposure and opaque contracting can reduce the state's effective control over strategic corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone and Border Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the Northwest and Southwest regions disrupts transport, agriculture, and local revenue collection. Instability along the Central African Republic and Lake Chad frontiers further raises the cost of securing resource routes.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security and Mining Nexus
frictionVectors.details: Russian-linked security personnel and commercial networks retain influence around regime protection and mineral access. Weak oversight makes it difficult for Bangui to convert gold and diamond production into transparent public revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Corridor and Border Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The country relies on fragile routes through Cameroon and neighboring states for imports and mineral exports. Armed groups and regional instability continue to constrain sovereign control beyond the capital.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Oil and Pipeline Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon revenues remain concentrated in a small number of projects and depend on foreign operators and the Cameroon export corridor. Price volatility, contract opacity, and weak downstream capacity limit domestic resource sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan War Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Refugee flows, arms trafficking, and cross-border armed activity from Sudan strain eastern Chad and divert state resources. N'Djamena continues to balance relationships with Western, Gulf, and regional security partners while preserving political autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: FRENCH SOVEREIGNTY DISPUTE
frictionVectors.details: France's control of Mayotte remains a persistent sovereignty grievance and constrains regional diplomacy. The dispute also affects migration, maritime boundaries, and access to surrounding resources.

frictionVectors.title: INFRASTRUCTURE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Limited domestic fiscal capacity leaves ports, energy, and transport development reliant on external donors and partners. This weakens national leverage over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: MINING SOVEREIGNTY
frictionVectors.details: Copper and cobalt remain central to global supply chains, but weak oversight, opaque contracts, and limited domestic processing reduce the state's share of value. Chinese, Western, and Gulf-linked interests compete for access.

frictionVectors.title: EASTERN SECURITY CORRIDOR
frictionVectors.details: Armed conflict involving M23 and regional actors continues to undermine Kinshasa's control over territory, trade routes, and mineral flows. External diplomatic and security pressure remains substantial.

frictionVectors.title: HYDROCARBON DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Oil revenues dominate export earnings and fiscal capacity, leaving sovereignty vulnerable to price cycles and foreign technical operators. Local value addition and economic diversification remain limited.

frictionVectors.title: INFRASTRUCTURE AND DEBT LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed construction and financing have expanded roads and public infrastructure while increasing exposure to external creditors and contractors. The government retains political control but has limited bargaining space.

frictionVectors.title: COCOA VALUE CHAIN
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire is improving farm-gate policy and processing capacity, but global buyers still capture much of the value and producer incomes remain vulnerable. Sustainability and deforestation rules from external markets add pressure.

frictionVectors.title: STRATEGIC PARTNER COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: France remains influential while China, Turkey, Gulf states, and other investors expand their roles in ports, energy, and construction. Abidjan is leveraging this competition but remains dependent on foreign capital and technology.

frictionVectors.title: BASES AND PORT LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: The concentration of foreign military facilities and competing port interests generates substantial revenue but limits Djibouti's strategic autonomy. Rivalry among the United States, China, France, and regional actors keeps infrastructure highly politicized.

frictionVectors.title: ETHIOPIAN CONNECTIVITY EXPOSURE
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti's economy depends heavily on Ethiopian trade and transport flows, creating leverage but also vulnerability to Ethiopian diversification and regional instability. Debt and infrastructure concentration further narrow policy flexibility.

frictionVectors.title: GERD and Nile Water Security
frictionVectors.details: Egypt continues to view Ethiopia's dam operations as a national-security issue. Diplomatic channels remain active, but the absence of a binding operating agreement sustains strategic friction.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing and Asset Influence
frictionVectors.details: IMF financing and Gulf investment support Egypt's balance of payments but increase outside leverage over ports, state assets, and infrastructure priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Oil and Gas Decline
frictionVectors.details: Maturing fields and limited diversification are weakening fiscal resilience. The government is seeking new offshore investment and gas-processing partnerships to preserve export capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Major infrastructure and energy projects rely heavily on foreign contractors and financing, particularly from Chinese and other external partners, limiting domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea Militarization
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline and proximity to shipping lanes attract competing regional and external security interests. Port access and regional rivalries create pressure on Asmara's non-aligned posture.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Revenue and Foreign Operators
frictionVectors.details: The mining sector remains dependent on foreign technical and capital partners, especially at major gold and copper operations. Opaque revenue arrangements and labor concerns continue to constrain sovereign legitimacy.

frictionVectors.title: SACU and South African Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Customs revenues, trade routes, energy supplies, and investment remain closely tied to South Africa and the wider SACU system. Any regional slowdown quickly narrows Eswatini's fiscal autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Political Legitimacy and Investment
frictionVectors.details: Political tensions and governance criticism complicate efforts to attract diversified foreign investment. This increases reliance on established external partners in manufacturing, sugar, and infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Debt Restructuring and External Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Debt-service pressures and restructuring negotiations limit policy space, while Chinese, Gulf, and Western financing remains important for infrastructure and foreign-exchange stability.

frictionVectors.title: Regional Infrastructure and Conflict
frictionVectors.details: Internal conflict risks disrupting transport, power, and industrial corridors. Tensions with Egypt and Sudan over Nile management and border security add external pressure to Ethiopia's development agenda.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Mining Concessions
frictionVectors.details: The transitional government is seeking greater state participation and local processing in manganese and other minerals, challenging established foreign operators. Renegotiation risks investment delays and diplomatic pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-Sector Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gabon remains reliant on foreign expertise and capital for mature offshore oil fields. Declining production limits the government's room to convert resource nationalism into durable fiscal sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Trade Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia's trade infrastructure remains vulnerable to external financing, regional logistics networks, and dependence on Senegalese routes. This constrains independent control over customs revenue and strategic commerce.

frictionVectors.title: Coastal Fisheries Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign industrial fishing and weak monitoring continue to challenge local control of marine resources. Fisheries enforcement capacity remains insufficient to prevent depletion and revenue leakage.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal Gold Mining
frictionVectors.details: Illegal mining damages waterways, agricultural land, and state legitimacy while creating openings for foreign financiers and illicit supply chains. Government efforts to formalize production face entrenched local and commercial interests.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Mining Finance
frictionVectors.details: Fiscal pressures and external financing requirements limit Accra's ability to impose tougher terms on multinational mining companies. New ambitions for local processing and lithium value chains remain dependent on outside capital and technology.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou External Leverage
frictionVectors.details: The Simandou iron-ore project is strengthening state bargaining power but remains dependent on foreign mining firms, Chinese infrastructure finance, and complex export logistics. The project could deepen raw-material dependence if domestic processing and revenue safeguards remain weak.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite Corridor Control
frictionVectors.details: Bauxite exports are dominated by foreign-backed operators and require extensive rail, port, and power infrastructure. Conakry's push for higher state participation is constrained by the capital intensity of the sector and military-government uncertainty.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew Value-Chain Capture
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains heavily dependent on raw cashew exports, leaving farmers and the state exposed to foreign buyers, price volatility, and limited domestic processing. Weak regulation reduces the government's ability to retain value locally.

frictionVectors.title: Bissau Port and Illicit Networks
frictionVectors.details: Limited port capacity, political instability, and alleged narcotics-trafficking networks undermine sovereign control over trade infrastructure. External security and commercial actors can therefore gain disproportionate influence over customs, logistics, and maritime access.

highlights: Port and Energy Sovereignty Under Pressure

frictionVectors.title: External Debt and Infrastructure Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Heavy obligations to international lenders and foreign infrastructure financiers constrain Nairobi's fiscal autonomy. The government is balancing Chinese, Western, Gulf, and multilateral interests while seeking to retain control over transport and energy assets.

frictionVectors.title: Lamu Corridor Security
frictionVectors.details: The Lamu port and transport corridor remain vulnerable to militant attacks, local grievances, and delays. Insecurity limits the corridor's value as a sovereign alternative to established regional trade routes.

frictionVectors.title: Lesotho Highlands Water Project
frictionVectors.details: Water exports to South Africa provide vital revenue but deepen structural dependence on Pretoria and external contractors. Project delays, cost overruns, and unequal benefit-sharing remain sensitive sovereignty issues.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Transport Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho remains highly dependent on South Africa for electricity, logistics, and market access. This limits its bargaining power over domestic resource development and regional infrastructure decisions.

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore and Mining Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Foreign mining firms dominate capital-intensive iron ore and gold operations, while Liberia seeks stronger local revenue, jobs, and processing commitments. Weak regulatory capacity increases the risk that resource gains remain externally captured.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Influence
frictionVectors.details: Control and financing of major ports and mineral corridors attract competing foreign commercial interests. The government must balance investment needs with fears of long-term concessions that reduce strategic control.

highlights: Foreign Powers Embedded in Energy Security

frictionVectors.title: Fragmented Oil Governance
frictionVectors.details: Competing political and armed authorities continue to contest budgets, appointments, and control of oil infrastructure. Production remains vulnerable to blockades and bargaining by local power centers.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Military and Energy Competition
frictionVectors.details: External actors support rival networks and seek influence over ports, security arrangements, and energy access. This reduces Libya's ability to set unified terms for infrastructure and resource partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: Nickel, Cobalt, and Ilmenite Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large mining projects are dominated by foreign capital and export-oriented supply chains, leaving Madagascar exposed to price swings and limited domestic value addition. Fiscal and environmental disputes challenge the state's ability to capture a larger share of mineral wealth.

frictionVectors.title: Ports and Strategic Connectivity
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed port, telecommunications, and transport projects are expanding Madagascar's external linkages but can create long-term dependence. Competition among Asian, Gulf, and Western investors complicates national infrastructure planning.

frictionVectors.title: External debt and conditionality
frictionVectors.details: Malawi remains heavily dependent on IMF and creditor support, limiting policy autonomy while restructuring external debt and managing foreign-exchange shortages.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: Uranium, rare-earth and niobium projects are attracting foreign investors, but weak infrastructure and regulatory capacity could leave the state with limited value capture.

highlights: Gold sector under tighter state control

frictionVectors.title: Russian security dependence
frictionVectors.details: The military government relies increasingly on Russian-linked security assistance, creating dependence while reducing Western leverage and complicating relations with regional institutions.

frictionVectors.title: Mining nationalism and insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Bamako is pressing foreign mining companies for greater state participation and revenue, but jihadist violence and transport insecurity continue to threaten production and export corridors.

frictionVectors.title: GTA gas project dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project with Senegal offers new revenue and diplomatic leverage, but offshore complexity, partner dependence and delayed production expose Mauritania to execution risks.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of logistics
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, European and Gulf actors remain important in mining, ports and infrastructure, raising concerns that iron and gas growth may reinforce enclave-style extraction.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos settlement implementation
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius is seeking to translate recognition of its sovereignty over the Chagos Archipelago into effective administrative and maritime gains while managing the future of the Diego Garcia base.

frictionVectors.title: External economic exposure
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains exposed to foreign investment, tourism and financial-sector scrutiny, leaving Mauritius vulnerable to shifts in European, Indian and global regulatory policy.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara sovereignty contest
frictionVectors.details: Morocco is converting diplomatic recognition and investment into de facto control of Western Sahara, while Algeria and the Polisario Front continue to contest the settlement.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign capital in strategic infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: European, Gulf and Chinese partners are central to ports, rail, energy and industrial projects; Rabat retains leverage but must manage dependency and technology-control risks.

highlights: Cabo Delgado LNG remains a sovereignty test

frictionVectors.title: LNG Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Mozambique relies heavily on foreign operators and external security support to protect northern gas assets. Insurgency and weak local benefit-sharing continue to limit effective state control.

frictionVectors.title: Resource-Corridor Inequality
frictionVectors.details: Ports, railways, and gas infrastructure are concentrated around externally financed corridors. Local communities remain vulnerable to displacement and limited participation in revenues.

highlights: Critical minerals and offshore oil raise strategic leverage

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Contract Pressure
frictionVectors.details: New offshore oil prospects are increasing competition among international energy firms for licenses and infrastructure access. Namibia is seeking stronger domestic participation without deterring investment.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Competition
frictionVectors.details: European, Gulf, Chinese, and South African actors are competing for influence over hydrogen, ports, logistics, and critical minerals. Windhoek retains comparatively strong bargaining capacity.

highlights: Junta asserts control over uranium and hydrocarbons
Security partnerships are shifting toward Russia

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Disputes
frictionVectors.details: The military government is renegotiating the terms of foreign mining involvement and presenting resource control as a sovereignty priority. Operational weakness and sanctions risk could still reduce state revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and Border Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: The oil-export corridor and major transport routes remain exposed to militant violence and political isolation. Reliance on new security partners has not eliminated infrastructure vulnerability.

highlights: Oil theft and grid weakness erode control

frictionVectors.title: Oil Theft and Production Losses
frictionVectors.details: Militancy, pipeline vandalism, and organized theft continue to undermine federal control of petroleum assets. International operators retain major technical and financial influence despite local-content gains.

frictionVectors.title: Power and Gas Infrastructure Gap
frictionVectors.details: Unreliable electricity and inadequate gas-processing capacity constrain industrial sovereignty. Foreign financing and private operators remain central to expanding energy infrastructure.

highlights: Regional security posture drives diplomatic friction

frictionVectors.title: Eastern Congo Mineral Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's regional security role and mineral-trading networks remain under intense scrutiny over alleged links to conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo. External pressure threatens market access and diplomatic room.

frictionVectors.title: Aid and Investment Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda has diversified investment and logistics partnerships but remains sensitive to Western aid conditionality and reputational risk. Its state-led development model provides control while limiting independent oversight.

frictionVectors.title: UNPROVEN OFFSHORE HYDROCARBONS
frictionVectors.details: Exploration in the Gulf of Guinea could create future fiscal leverage, but São Tomé and Príncipe has no commercial production and remains vulnerable to unfavorable terms if discoveries occur.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL FINANCE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Portuguese, and multilateral financing support infrastructure and public services, limiting the island state's room to negotiate independently.

highlights: Oil and gas sovereignty is being renegotiated

frictionVectors.title: HYDROCARBON CONTRACTS
frictionVectors.details: Sangomar and Greater Tortue Ahmeyim production offers Dakar greater leverage, but foreign operators, financing structures, and existing contracts constrain how quickly the state can increase its share.

frictionVectors.title: FISHERIES AND COASTAL PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: Industrial fishing access, coastal development, and offshore energy expansion are creating friction over livelihoods, local content, and control of marine resources.

frictionVectors.title: FOREIGN FISHING ACCESS
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles benefits from licensing revenue and tuna-sector investment, but dependence on foreign fleets complicates enforcement and long-term control of maritime resources.

frictionVectors.title: INDIAN OCEAN STRATEGIC COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Indian, Chinese, European, and other security and infrastructure interests provide useful support while exposing the archipelago to pressure over ports, maritime surveillance, and strategic alignment.

highlights: Mining remains the economic power center

frictionVectors.title: IRON ORE AND RAIL CONCESSIONS
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale mining and associated rail and port infrastructure can generate national revenue, but foreign operators retain substantial influence over logistics, pricing, and project governance.

frictionVectors.title: ILLICIT AND INFORMAL MINING
frictionVectors.details: Unregulated diamond, gold, rutile, and other mineral activity weakens state oversight, fuels local disputes, and reduces public capture of resource rents.

highlights: Offshore hydrocarbons are becoming geopolitical assets

frictionVectors.title: TURKEY AND OFFSHORE ENERGY
frictionVectors.details: Turkish security and energy cooperation strengthens Mogadishu's bargaining position, but the federal government's limited territorial control makes future offshore concessions politically and operationally contested.

frictionVectors.title: SOMALILAND AND REGIONAL ACCESS
frictionVectors.details: Disputes involving Somaliland, Ethiopia, and Red Sea access complicate Somalia's claims over ports, maritime zones, and prospective resource areas while inviting competing external sponsors.

highlights: Critical-minerals leverage, constrained by power and rail
Strategic autonomy amid competing external partnerships

frictionVectors.title: Power and freight infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Electricity reliability and rail-port bottlenecks limit domestic control over mineral value chains. Private-sector investment and foreign technology remain important to recovery.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: The United States, China, and European partners are competing for battery and platinum-group mineral access, creating pressure for Pretoria to balance nonalignment with investment needs.

highlights: Oil revenue remains the state’s strategic lifeline

frictionVectors.title: Oil-export vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan depends on transit infrastructure through Sudan, leaving production and public revenue exposed to conflict, sabotage, and bargaining by external and neighboring actors.

frictionVectors.title: Elite-controlled resource governance
frictionVectors.details: Weak institutions and patronage networks limit transparent management of oil income, while external security and commercial partners retain leverage over core infrastructure.

highlights: War has fragmented control of national resources
Red Sea access is a strategic external prize

frictionVectors.title: Gold and wartime finance
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and trade help finance rival military networks, with foreign buyers and regional intermediaries benefiting from weak oversight and contested territory.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Control of Port Sudan, oil-transit routes, and humanitarian corridors is tied to military survival and external influence, particularly across the Red Sea and Gulf networks.

highlights: Infrastructure diplomacy is expanding sovereign capacity

frictionVectors.title: Mining-contract leverage
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is seeking greater local processing, fiscal returns, and state participation in critical minerals while managing investor concerns over regulatory unpredictability.

frictionVectors.title: Rail and port dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Standard Gauge Railway and port expansions strengthen regional connectivity, but financing, construction, and operating partnerships leave continued exposure to foreign capital and contractors.

highlights: Lomé remains a key regional logistics hub

frictionVectors.title: Port and trade concentration
frictionVectors.details: Togo’s economic sovereignty is closely tied to the Port of Lomé and its role in serving landlocked neighbors, leaving customs, shipping, and corridor disruptions strategically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Northern security pressure
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist spillover from the Sahel is driving expanded security cooperation and border controls, increasing reliance on external training, intelligence, and equipment.

frictionVectors.title: EU Migration Partnership
frictionVectors.details: European financial support and migration cooperation give the EU significant leverage over Tunisia's border policy and domestic political choices.

frictionVectors.title: Gas and Power Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia remains dependent on imported energy and external financing while seeking to expand domestic renewables and maintain electricity stability.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP Sovereignty Dispute
frictionVectors.details: The Tilenga and East African Crude Oil Pipeline projects promise state revenue but expose Uganda to environmental criticism, sanctions pressure, and dependence on foreign operators and capital.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure Financing Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed transport and energy infrastructure strengthens Uganda's development capacity while increasing long-term exposure to external lenders and contractors.

frictionVectors.title: Copper Value-Chain Control
frictionVectors.details: Lusaka is pushing for greater local processing and transparency, but foreign firms still dominate capital, technology, and access to global copper markets.

frictionVectors.title: Lobito Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: Western-backed rail and logistics links offer diversification from traditional southern routes, while Chinese commercial interests remain deeply embedded in Zambia's mining infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Lithium Concession Race
frictionVectors.details: Zimbabwe is restricting raw lithium exports to encourage domestic processing, but Chinese firms retain a commanding position across mining, refining, and associated infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Sanctions Entrapment
frictionVectors.details: Western sanctions and arrears limit access to conventional finance, pushing Harare toward opaque arrangements with Chinese, Russian, and regional partners for resource-backed investment.
